title: Greenwashing Decoder
summary: A reference for the language brands use when they want to suggest virtue without committing to it. Each term shows what brands typically claim and what the term actually means.

terms.claim: Often implies "good for you" or "safe", suggesting wholesome plant origin.
terms.actual: In most jurisdictions there is no legal definition of "natural" in cosmetics or food labelling. Arsenic, lead, and poison ivy are also "natural".
terms.src: US FTC: "no clear definition"; EU food law: no harmonised meaning.

terms.claim: The product is gentle on the environment.
terms.actual: Considered too vague to substantiate by the US FTC. The Green Guides require any environmental claim be qualified with what specifically is eco-friendly and how.

terms.claim: The product breaks down naturally and harmlessly.
terms.actual: Must be qualified — biodegradable under what conditions? Within what timeframe? Most "biodegradable" plastics require industrial composting (60°C+) which most consumers cannot access.
terms.src: FTC Green Guides §260.8; EU EN 13432 standard.

terms.claim: You can compost the packaging at home.
terms.actual: Usually means industrially compostable, not home-compostable. Distinguish between BPI / TUV "OK Compost HOME" certification and "OK Compost INDUSTRIAL".

Only meaningful if recycling facilities for the specific material are available to most consumers in your region. Theoretically recyclable ≠ practically recycled. Globally, less than 9% of all plastic ever made has been recycled.

Not legally defined globally. May refer to the finished product but not individual ingredients, or only to the manufacturer’s own labs not third-party testing. Look for Leaping Bunny or PETA Beauty Without Bunnies certification.
terms.src: EU Cosmetics Reg banned animal-tested cosmetics from sale since 2013; cruelty-free labelling unregulated.

terms.actual: In cosmetics, not legally defined — but a "vegan" label generally means no animal-derived ingredients. It does NOT mean cruelty-free.

terms.claim: Doesn’t harm the environment over time.
terms.actual: No regulatory definition. The UN Brundtland definition is "meeting the needs of the present without compromising future generations" — meaningless as a product label.

terms.claim: The company has zero net carbon emissions.
terms.actual: Almost always achieved through carbon offsets, not actual emission reductions. Many offset schemes have been investigated for over-claiming. The EU proposes banning the term unless backed by science-based reductions.
terms.src: EU Green Claims Directive (2023 proposal); Guardian/Die Zeit/SourceMaterial Verra investigation (2023).

terms.actual: Usually depends on offsets and assumed future negative-emissions technology. The SBTi Net-Zero Standard sets criteria (90%+ absolute reduction by 2050) but few corporate "net-zero" claims meet it.
No regulatory threshold. "Plant-based" can mean 100% plant or "contains some plants" depending on the product.
No regulatory definition. Each retailer (Sephora, Credo, Ulta) sets its own "clean" criteria — they don’t agree with each other.
In the EU, "free-range" eggs require 4m² per hen of outdoor access — but only theoretical access; many never go outside. For meat, the term is less regulated. UK definitions are similar.
Legally defined in EU and US — requires certification (USDA Organic, EU Organic logo). The term itself, alone, on a product is regulated. But "organic" cosmetic claims are less tightly controlled.

terms.claim: Workers received fair wages and conditions.
terms.actual: Several certifications exist (Fairtrade International, Fair Trade USA, World Fair Trade Organization) with different standards. "Fair trade" without certification is meaningless.
No regulatory definition of "local". Some EU/UK retailers define it as within 30 miles or within county — but the term on packaging is unregulated.
Dose-dependent and undefined. The FTC Green Guides require substantiation for non-toxic claims; the EU has prohibited the unqualified use of "non-toxic" on detergents and cleaning products.
terms.src: FTC Green Guides §260.10; EU Detergents Regulation.

terms.actual: Comparative claims require disclosure of the comparison basis. "Greener than what?" "More sustainable than which version?" — must be substantiated.
terms.src: FTC Green Guides §260.4; UK CMA Green Claims Code 2021.

terms.claim: The factory runs on solar/wind etc.
terms.actual: May refer to purchased Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) that don’t actually power the factory. Look for guarantees of additionality and physical delivery.
Marketing language only. No regulatory meaning. The UK ASA and EU Green Claims Directive both flag these as unsubstantiated vagueness.

terms.claim: Materials and labour meet fair standards.
terms.actual: No legal definition and no required certification. Without a named standard (Fairtrade, SA8000, WFTO) it is an unverifiable marketing phrase.
Undefined and self-declared. ‘Responsible’ sets no measurable bar — ask: responsible to whom, verified by whom?

terms.claim: This sunscreen won’t harm coral reefs.
terms.actual: There is no standardised or regulated definition of ‘reef-safe’. Check the actual filters — avoid oxybenzone and octinoxate rather than trusting the label.

terms.claim: Made from plastic rescued from the sea.
terms.actual: Usually means plastic collected within ~50 km of a coastline — not from the ocean itself. Definitions vary by certifier and are often generous.
Can mean as little as 1% recycled content. Look for a stated percentage and whether it is post-consumer (used by people) or pre-consumer (factory offcuts).
Scientifically impossible — water is a chemical. The term is meaningless and flagged as misleading by regulators.
terms.src: UK ASA rulings; EU Green Claims Directive.

terms.actual: Only means a dermatologist was involved in testing — not that it passed, nor how many people, nor the result. ‘Tested’ is not ‘approved’.
No federal standard or required testing in the US. Manufacturers define it themselves. Any product can be labelled hypoallergenic.

terms.claim: The animal ate only grass, on pasture.
terms.actual: In many markets animals may be ‘grass-fed’ yet grain-finished, or fed grass indoors. ‘100% grass-fed’ and pasture certifications are stricter.

terms.claim: Hens roam freely, not in cages.
terms.actual: Means hens are uncaged inside a barn — not that they go outdoors or have much space. Distinct from free-range or pasture-raised.
Not legally defined in most markets. Meaningful only with a third-party welfare certification (e.g. RSPCA Assured, Certified Humane, GAP).
Marketing shorthand with no definition. Each brand decides what a ‘nasty’ is — often to imply competitors are unsafe.
terms.src: UK ASA / EU Green Claims Directive.

terms.claim: No trees were cut for this paper.
terms.actual: Can be true (bamboo, sugarcane bagasse) but doesn’t address the water, land, or transport footprint of the alternative crop. Verify the whole picture.

terms.claim: The product removes more carbon than it emits.
terms.actual: Almost always relies on offsets rather than actual removals, and ‘positive’ claims are even harder to substantiate than ‘neutral’ ones. The EU proposes restricting both.

terms.claim: Contains no palm oil, so it’s better for forests.
terms.actual: Sometimes true, but replacements (coconut, soy, shea) can need MORE land. Certified sustainable palm (RSPO) can be a lower-impact choice than a blanket boycott.
No definition of ‘small’ or ‘artisan’. Large manufacturers use these terms freely to imply craft and care.
